claims.text: The Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy is obtained by removing Co from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
Both the Co-free FeNiCrMn alloy and the CoCrFeMnNi baseline are as-solidified, single-phase solid solutions.
Removing Co from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi increases the stacking-fault energy sufficiently to delay deformation twinning.
Stacking-fault energy mediates the balance between dislocation slip and deformation twinning.
Higher stacking-fault energy makes twinning less favorable and promotes dislocation motion relative to mechanical twinning.
Co removal causes FeNiCrMn to shift from twin-assisted strain hardening toward dislocation-glide-dominated deformation.
Deformation twins can act as barriers to dislocation motion and contribute to strength and strain hardening.
Fewer deformation twins in FeNiCrMn will reduce the twinning contribution to strain hardening.
Relative to CoCrFeMnNi, FeNiCrMn will require lower temperatures or higher strain rates to trigger twinning.
FeNiCrMn will have lower twin density than CoCrFeMnNi under comparable loading conditions.
FeNiCrMn will show modified flow stress–strain behavior, including reduced strain hardening attributable to twinning.
Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi exhibits early twinning at lower temperatures and strain rates.
Twinning contributes significantly to the strength–ductility balance of equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi.
The proposed comparison varies strain rate from approximately 10^-5 to 10^-2 s^-1 and temperature from cryogenic or room temperature to elevated temperature under identical protocols.
Twin density and dislocation structures can be compared during loading using EBSD and TEM alongside stress–strain measurements.
The hypothesis is restricted to as-solidified, single-phase alloys and may not apply after heat treatment, precipitation, or other microstructural modification.
Comparable twinning onset, twin density, and dislocation structure in the two alloys under identical conditions would falsify the proposed Co-removal mechanism.
